messages.content: Argue that aesthetic value cannot be coherently reduced to purely subjective preference or individual psychological response. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) the phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience involves a claim to intersubjective validity — when we judge a work beautiful we implicitly call on others to agree, a normative dimension that a purely subjectivist framework cannot explain; (2) the practice of aesthetic criticism — with its apparatus of reasons, standards, and education — presupposes that aesthetic assessments are answerable to considerations beyond individual response, and that some responses are better-informed than others; (3) aesthetic relativism generates a regress: if every preference is equally valid, then the preference for pluralism over dogmatism is itself merely a preference, undermining the normative force of the relativist position from within. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

message.content:
When one experiences a work of art as genuinely beautiful, the judgment carries with it an implicit demand that others ought to share in that appreciation, rather than treating the response as a mere private sensation. This phenomenological feature of aesthetic experience points to a normative claim of intersubjective validity, suggesting that the beauty is there to be recognized by any suitably attuned perceiver. A framework that reduces aesthetic value entirely to subjective preference struggles to account for this dimension, as it would render such calls for agreement inexplicable or merely rhetorical. 

The ongoing practices of aesthetic criticism rely on the possibility of offering reasons and appealing to standards that transcend individual tastes, allowing for education in appreciation and the distinction between more and less informed responses. Critics engage in detailed analysis and comparison precisely because they assume that assessments can be improved through attention to relevant features of the work, rather than being insulated within personal psychology. This institutional reality indicates that aesthetic judgments are responsive to considerations that can be shared and debated, undermining any strict reduction to isolated subjective states.

The position of aesthetic relativism encounters an internal difficulty, for if all preferences are deemed equally valid without further grounding, then the relativist's own advocacy for tolerance or pluralism over rigid dogmatism amounts to nothing more than another preference without special authority. This creates a regress in which the normative force required to sustain the relativist stance against alternative views cannot be consistently maintained, revealing the position's inability to provide a coherent alternative to objectivist understandings of aesthetic value.
message.reasoning:
The task requires an argument against reducing aesthetic value to purely subjective preference or individual psychological response.

The first claim holds that genuine aesthetic experience implicitly demands intersubjective agreement, a normative dimension that purely subjective frameworks cannot explain. The second claims that aesthetic criticism presupposes standards and reasons beyond individual response, and that some responses are better-informed than others.

The third claim exposes a regress in aesthetic relativism. If every preference is equally valid, then the preference for pluralism over dogmatism is itself merely a preference. This undermines the normative force of the relativist position from within.

The essay will be structured as a continuous flowing argument across three paragraphs. The first paragraph introduces the thesis and establishes the first claim. It then transitions smoothly into the second claim. The third claim follows in the final paragraph.

The opening paragraph frames aesthetic judgment as an implicit demand for intersubjective agreement, not a private sensation. It suggests that genuine beauty is recognized by any suitably attuned perceiver.

A purely subjective framework cannot explain this demand for agreement. It would treat such calls as mere rhetoric. Aesthetic criticism depends on standards and reasons that transcend individual taste. This allows education in appreciation and distinguishes more informed responses from less.
